St Margaret's Hampstead
We are preparing for life
An Exceptional Education for Girls in the Heart of Hampstead
A leading independent school for girls aged 4–16
A small school with a huge heart. Like most schools, we want our girls to be happy, well-rounded and confident, and for them to do their very best academically. At St Margaret's Hampstead, we reach these goals by engaging with each girl on a very personal level, which is something you can do when you have small classes, low teacher turnover and a culture of involvement.
We are delighted to announce that we were voted Number 1 in The Sunday Times league tables for schools without a Sixth Form, 2023.
Meet the students
Where every girl stands out
Here, it is not only the tallest, most athletic girls who represent the school at netball or the most extrovert who get the speaking roles in plays. Everyone is valued, and we encourage and celebrate excellence and enthusiasm in equally high measure. Every girl is involved in the life and experiences that the school has to offer.

A forward-thinking independent school in north London
St Margaret’s Hampstead is a dynamic girls’ school where ambition meets care. Our broad curriculum, expert teachers and exceptional pastoral support create an education that empowers girls to think independently, take risks and become compassionate leaders.
With strong results, a thriving co-curricular programme and a warm, family-centred community, this is a school where every girl is encouraged to shine.
Taught by experts
We recruit and retain the very best teachers in order to ensure that the teaching and learning throughout the school are exceptional, and our staff turnover is very low. We also focus closely on our staff's understanding of the importance of pastoral care in creating a harmonious community.
Practical & prepared
Respect for others lies at the heart of the school community, where the potential and talent of each individual can be recognised, nurtured and realised. At St Margaret's Hampstead, education is seen as a partnership between pupils, parents and teachers.

pageCache.pageTitle: Our Ethos & Values | A Nurturing Education in Hampstead
pageCache.text:
Our Ethos & Values: Preparing for Life, in a Kind Way
At St Margaret’s Hampstead, our unique approach to education is captured by our motto, 'Ad Vitam Paramus' - Latin for “Preparing for Life.” This is more than a slogan; it is a philosophy that guides everything we do. As described by The Good Schools Guide, we offer a “cosy, nurturing, rounded and grounded education delivered in a happy family atmosphere”.
We believe that a truly transformative education balances academic rigour with a profound commitment to personal wellbeing, preparing girls not just for examinations, but for a life of confidence, resilience and intellectual curiosity. In the competitive educational landscape of North London, we offer a different path – a kinder way of getting there.
“Afford them time to offer more help to each girl in the room”– ISI Inspection
The heart of our community: exceptional pastoral care
Our commitment to pastoral care is at the heart of our school's identity. The appointment of our new Head, Sharron Shackell, whose background is rooted in pastoral leadership, sends a clear message about our dedication to this core value.Our intimate scale is the secret to our success. With an average class size of 14, and an excellent pupil-to-teacher ratio, every girl is known, seen and supported.Our genuine family feel is an organic, lived experience, creating an environment where every girl has an innate sense of belonging and feels safe to take on new challenges. This is evidenced by an ISI inspection report, which found that pupils reported that our "effective pastoral care systems help them to find a resolution" when issues arise.For girls with moderate learning needs such as dyslexia or dyspraxia, our small classes are our primary mechanism of support. The majority of girls' needs are addressed directly by their teachers, as our ISI report highlight the small class sizes "afford them time to offer more help to each girl in the room". This integrated approach ensures that personalised care is a core part of daily instruction.
Academic excellence without the pressure
In a city defined by selective entry, we are proud to be a non-selective school with excellent academic outcomes. Our GCSE results are a testament to our approach, with 65 per cent of grades in 2025 at 9–7.What truly sets us apart is our proven ability to add significant value. Value-added data, stretching back over a decade, shows that St Margaret's Hampstead girls make notably more progress than pupils of similar abilities attending other schools. This is the ultimate proof that our nurturing environment is a direct driver of academic success.
By deliberately avoiding the often-crushing pressure of going through the 11+ transfer process, we are free to focus on instilling a deep love for learning. This gives our girls the confidence to take risks and try for high-achieving schools post-GCSE.
The St Margaret’s girl
Our ethos culminates in the character of our students. A St Margaret's girl is confident, resilient and grounded, with an innate sense of belonging.We celebrate every achievement, whether in academics, sports or the arts, and recognise that each girl will take her own individual path to success. Our personalised approach, enabled by our small classes, ensures that every girl's unique talents and aspirations are seen, supported and celebrated.The result is a community where kindness and respect are paramount, and where every girl is prepared for a life of purpose and contribution.
Experience the St Margaret’s Hampstead difference for your daughter
We invite you to discover firsthand how St Margaret's Hampstead can inspire your daughter's journey. Join our vibrant community where every girl is empowered to achieve her full potential.

A Warm Welcome From Our Head Sharron Shackell
It is with immense pride and excitement that I introduce myself as the Head of St Margaret’s Hampstead. Stepping into this role, I am deeply committed to upholding and enriching the unique spirit that defines our school – a place where every girl is truly known, valued and inspired to achieve her personal best.My educational philosophy is rooted in the belief that a truly exceptional education balances rigorous academic pursuit with comprehensive pastoral care. I believe that when girls feel genuinely happy, secure and understood, they are empowered to embrace challenges, explore their passions and develop into confident, compassionate and well-rounded individuals ready for the world beyond our gates. This holistic approach, nurturing both intellectual curiosity and emotional resilience, is at the very heart of St Margaret’s Hampstead.
A foundation of experience & dedication
On a personal note, I live in Hertfordshire with my husband and our three teenage daughters, giving me a deep understanding of the joys and complexities of family life and the importance of choosing the right educational home. My journey in education spans over two decades – a career dedicated to nurturing young minds and creating environments where students thrive. I earned a First Class degree in History and Politics from the University of Manchester, followed by my PGCE in History from the prestigious University of Cambridge. This strong academic foundation has underpinned my extensive teaching career.Prior to joining St Margaret’s Hampstead, I served as Deputy Head (Pastoral) at Immanuel College in Bushey, Hertfordshire, an HMC all-through school. This role, alongside my previous position as Director of Sixth Form, has provided me with extensive expertise in both academic leadership and, crucially, in developing robust pastoral care systems that support the wellbeing of every student. My commitment to educational excellence extends beyond the classroom – I am also an Independent Schools Inspectorate inspector and have proudly served as a governor at the Royal Masonic School for Girls in Hertfordshire since 2019. These experiences offer me a unique perspective on best practices in independent education across the UK.
Nurturing future leaders in Hampstead
With its commitment to small classes and a personalised approach, St Margaret’s Hampstead offers an unparalleled environment for girls aged 4–16 to flourish. I am excited to build upon our legacy of academic achievement, ensuring our girls are exceptionally prepared for entry into leading Sixth Forms in London and beyond. We will continue to champion a vibrant co-curricular life, encouraging every girl to discover her unique talents in sports, arts and a diverse range of clubs.My vision for St Margaret’s Hampstead is one of continuous growth – not just in academic results, but in the character, confidence and compassion of our students. We will continue to cultivate a strong, supportive community where girls feel empowered to be curious, kind and courageous, ready to make a positive impact on the world.
Join our St Margaret’s Hampstead family
I warmly invite you to visit St Margaret’s Hampstead to experience our vibrant atmosphere firsthand. Come and meet our dedicated staff and, most importantly, our wonderful girls. I look forward to welcoming you and sharing more about how St Margaret’s Hampstead can inspire your daughter’s journey.

Board of Governors
The Governors of the School, who are also Trustees of the charity that operates it, determine the aims, strategy and overall conduct of the school. They set and review the policies, plans and procedures that will ensure the best possible education for present and future pupils of St Margaret's Hampstead. They are responsible for legal and regulatory compliance and risk management, financial propriety, strategic direction, the maintenance of standards and the guardianship of the charity's assets. Responsibility for the day-to-day management of the school is delegated to the Head.

pageCache.pageTitle: 7 Ways Executive Function Skills Build Independent Learners
pageCache.text:
7 Ways Executive Function Skills in Children Build Independent Learners
Executive function in children shapes the way they plan, organise, focus, adapt and manage their emotions throughout school life. These self-regulation skills support everything from remembering homework instructions to navigating friendships and managing exam preparation.
Neuroscience research links executive function skills to activity in the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain responsible for planning, working memory, cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control. Studies continue to highlight the relationship between executive function and academic achievement, emotional wellbeing and long-term independence.
For children, executive function acts like an air traffic control system. It helps them prioritise information, manage distractions, organise tasks and regulate responses throughout the day.
At St Margaret’s Hampstead, we develop these skills through our curriculum, pastoral care and co-curricular opportunities from the early years through to GCSE study. Here, we'll take you through how executive function skills build independent learners and how we nurture them across school life.
1. Working memory helps pupils manage complex learning
Working memory allows children to hold and use information in real time. Pupils rely on it when solving maths problems, following multi-step instructions, reading comprehension tasks and preparing written work.
Executive function measures consistently show that strong working memory supports academic progress across multiple subjects, particularly literacy and numeracy.
At St Margaret’s, our small class sizes give teachers time to check understanding, reinforce key concepts and tailor learning to each pupil’s needs. This supports pupils as they strengthen working memory and develop confidence in independent study.
Our Junior School curriculum introduces structured learning routines early on, helping girls retain information, organise ideas and apply knowledge across subjects. Our specialist-taught music education also supports executive function development. Reading musical symbols, learning music theory and performing as part of an ensemble all engage working memory and attention control simultaneously. Musical training strengthens concentration and sequencing skills that pupils carry into the wider curriculum.
2. Cognitive flexibility helps children adapt and problem solve
Cognitive flexibility allows pupils to shift between ideas, adjust to new information and approach challenges from different perspectives. Children use this executive function skill every day in the classroom, particularly during creative writing, scientific investigation and collaborative projects.
At St Margaret’s, our broad curriculum encourages girls to think creatively, debate ideas confidently and approach learning with curiosity. Through classroom discussion, project work and enrichment activities, pupils learn how to adapt their thinking and develop problem-solving skills, which enhances cognitive flexibility.
Our Senior School environment supports this progression further by preparing girls for GCSE study through independent research, analytical thinking and leadership opportunities.
Outdoor learning also plays an important role. Our forest school sessions encourage pupils to navigate unfamiliar situations, assess risks and make decisions collaboratively. Studies exploring physical activity and executive function highlight links between movement, self-regulation skills and improved cognitive flexibility and performance.
3. Inhibitory control supports focus and emotional regulation
Inhibitory control refers to a child’s ability to pause, think and regulate their responses. This executive function skill supports concentration, classroom behaviour and emotional self-management.
Children use inhibitory control when they wait their turn, resist distractions or manage frustration during challenging tasks. Response inhibition also plays a significant role in attention and learning.
At St Margaret’s, pastoral care forms a central part of school life because emotional security supports learning. Girls who feel supported and understood are more likely to develop confidence, resilience and self-regulation skills.
Our teachers build strong relationships with pupils throughout their educational journey, allowing girls to develop trust, independence and emotional awareness within a familiar environment.
4. Organisational skills help pupils become independent learners
Organisation sits at the heart of executive function in children. Independent learners need to manage deadlines, prioritise tasks, track responsibilities and prepare effectively for assessments. Children develop these skills gradually through structured routines, consistent expectations and opportunities for responsibility.
At St Margaret’s, we encourage girls to take ownership of their learning from an early age. Teachers guide pupils through time management strategies, revision planning and goal setting so they develop habits that support long-term academic success.
Visual reminders, checklists and structured classroom routines support younger pupils as they develop executive function skills. Older pupils manage independent projects, homework schedules and revision timetables with greater autonomy.
Our all-through structure also supports continuity across key stages. Girls remain within a familiar environment where teachers understand their strengths, learning styles and developmental needs.
5. Social connection strengthens executive function development
Children develop executive function through relationships, communication and shared early experiences. Positive developmental environments support emotional regulation, attention and social awareness throughout childhood.
At St Margaret’s, our girls learn within a close-knit community where friendships, mentoring opportunities and collaborative learning form part of daily life. Child-to-child mentoring and peer support through our Family Tree encourages girls to communicate clearly, solve problems together and build confidence socially as well as academically.
Co-curricular activities also contribute significantly to executive function development. Drama productions, debating, sport and musical performance all strengthen planning, focus, teamwork and emotional regulation.
Our co-curricular programme encourages every girl to participate fully, helping pupils discover new strengths and develop independence across many areas of school life.
6. Consistent routines help pupils feel secure and confident
Children thrive when they understand expectations and feel emotionally secure. Predictable routines support executive function by reducing cognitive overload and helping pupils focus their attention effectively.
At St Margaret’s, consistency supports every stage of learning. Girls move through school with familiar routines, trusted adults and clear expectations that help them feel secure and confident.
Our teachers understand that children develop executive function gradually across childhood and adolescence. Through encouragement, structure and personalised support, we help girls strengthen these skills steadily over time. This continuity becomes especially valuable during periods of transition, including the move into Senior School and preparation for their GCSEs.
7. Executive function skills prepare girls for life beyond school
Executive function skills shape how children manage responsibilities, build relationships, solve problems and navigate new situations independently. Strong executive function supports leadership, communication, resilience and self-motivation throughout adulthood.
At St Margaret’s, we prepare girls for life with the confidence to think independently, communicate clearly and approach challenges positively. Through our curriculum, pastoral care and co-curricular opportunities, girls develop the executive function skills that support academic success and personal growth throughout every stage of education.
Not only do our girls leave St Margaret's prepared for the demands of further and higher education and the world of work, but they also are near-enough guaranteed to secure a place at their chosen sixth form.
Frequently asked questions
What is executive function in children?
Executive function refers to a set of mental skills that help children plan, organise, focus, remember instructions and regulate their behaviour. These skills include working memory, cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control.
Why are executive function skills important for learning?
Executive function skills are important for learning because they help pupils manage tasks independently, stay organised, solve problems and focus during lessons. These skills also support emotional regulation, resilience and academic achievement.
At what age do executive function skills develop?
Executive function skills begin developing in early childhood and continue strengthening throughout adolescence. Schools play an important role in supporting this development through structured routines, problem-solving activities and opportunities for independence.
How can schools support executive function in children?
Schools support executive function through structured learning, consistent routines, personalised teaching, co-curricular activities and strong pastoral care. Activities including music, sport, outdoor learning and collaborative projects also contribute positively to executive function development and its key components, including cognitive flexibility, working memory and inhibitory control.

pageCache.pageTitle: 8 Benefits of All-Through Girls Schools | St Margaret's
pageCache.text:
8 Benefits of All-Through Girls Schools
One of the many decisions you'll make about your child's education is whether to send them to separate primary and secondary schools, or whether to opt for an all-through school.
Schools that educate children from Reception through to Year 11 offer a lot of benefits from students, from a consistent curriculum to reduced stress because of fewer school transitions.
The benefits are especially strong for all-through single sex schools for girls, as they can build confidence and pursue their passions without the gender stereotyping that is common in mixed-sex schools.
Here, we'll take you through the benefits of all-through schools for girls to help you make an informed decision about your daughter's education.
1. Seamless progression through school
The hallmark of an all-through school is that it offers a seamless journey through all compulsory educational stages. This means your daughter will remain at the same institution from Reception (or sometimes Nursery) right through until she sits her GCSEs, and sometimes into sixth form.
This smooth journey means your daughter will experience familiar surroundings throughout her educational journey. She doesn't need to worry about a new campus or school culture or making new friends in key stages 2 or 3, whereas pupils at primary and secondary schools may need to do this.
This familiarity means your daughter will spend less mental energy on learning new routines, classes and forming new relationships. In an all-through school, she can instead put that focus into her education.
2. Reduced stress due to fewer transitions
Transitioning to different schools at each key stage can be a stressful experience. Girls will be leaving a comfortable and familiar environment and entering one that's completely new to them, plus they may have to contend with new social groups and making new friends from scratch.
This can be especially stressful for anxious, socially awkward or introverted children who benefit from stable surroundings in terms of their physical spaces and the people around them. An all-through school takes these transitions away, meaning that there's less stress placed on your daughter as she progresses through school.
Some schools may split their junior and senior schools into different campuses, but your daughter will still benefit from the same peer groups and some of the same staff at her school. At St Margaret's Hampstead, your daughter will benefit from the same school spaces in infant, junior and senior school until she moves onto further education, allowing her to thrive in a space that is familiar to her.
3. Long-standing relationships with teachers and peers
One of the key aspects of stability in all-through schools is the long-term relationships your daughter will build with her friends and peers. It's highly likely that a lot of the students that start school with her in Reception or Year 1 will still be with her by Year 11, meaning she can build strong and meaningful friendships that are consistent throughout her school experience. There are also student-to-student mentoring opportunities, like our Family Tree at St Margaret's, where older pupils support younger girls and help build their confidence.
Your daughter will also benefit from having access to a lot of the same members of staff in areas like pastoral care. This is especially important because your daughter won't need to build trust with new support staff if she experiences any issues or needs any support, creating a secure educational environment.
While students will most likely be taught by different specialist teachers in different key stages at an all-through school, they'll have opportunities to interact with their future teachers. What's more, early years teachers will share their progress, strengths and areas for improvement with their future teachers to ensure a continuous educational journey. This continuity of friends and teachers creates a strong and long-lasting sense of community in your daughter's all-through school.
4. Reduced exposure to gender stereotypes throughout education
One of the most well-established benefits of all-girls' all-through schools is that they are less limiting for girls than mixed-sex schools. Without the constraints of gender stereotypes and unconscious biases pushing them towards certain subjects, girls can excel in subjects traditionally designated for boys. Girls also achieve better grades in single-sex schools compared to mixed-gender environments.
It's been proven that girls who attend single-sex schools are more assertive, confident and are more likely to pursue leadership opportunities. This is largely because of the nurturing school cultures in all-girls' environments and the ability to take up more space without being drowned out by male peers. Additionally, girls are exposed to female role models in all-girls' schools, which can help them see that anything is possible.
These benefits are specific to all-girls schools and are enhanced when girls attend an all-through school from the early years to Year 11. By consistently learning in an environment that gives them the space to be themselves, speak out and pursue their passions throughout their education, girls leave school well-prepared for the demands of further education and the world of work. All-through girls schools also offer specialist facilities including sports centres and forest school, so girls can pursue their passions without the concerns of boys detracting from their skills.
5. No entrance exam pressure
When students stay at the same independent school throughout their whole compulsory education, they don't have to deal with the stress that comes with entrance exams. Some parents, when exploring independent education, will opt for prep schools, which prepare students for selective secondary education.
However, these entrance exams can be a great source of pressure and stress for students. Instead, you should explore the credentials of all-through schools to see if they can offer your daughter the benefits that selective secondary schools can. Often, you'll find that is the case.
At St Margaret's, 56% of our girls achieved grades 7–9 in their GCSEs in 2025, doubling the London average of 28% and almost trebling the UK-wide average of 21.8%. What's more, all of our girls secured places in their chosen sixth forms.
6. Curriculum continuity
One risk of sending your child to multiple separate schools is the shift in curriculum and teaching that they'll experience. All-through schools have one defined curriculum and teaching method that is consistent throughout the years. This means that your daughter won't have to spend time getting used to different learning methodologies or a completely new curriculum.
This consistent learning experience means students will continually build upon existing knowledge in a way they're familiar with. Teachers from different year groups and key stages will work together to make sure that students can transition from one stage to the next smoothly and without friction.
7. Stable learning environment offering emotional security
When your daughter learns in one place and sees the same familiar faces every day, it offers a sense of emotional security. This feeling of emotional safety is essential to girls as they develop; they need to know that they will be supported and that they can trust their teachers and other adults in their life.
This becomes even more important as girls transition into puberty and experience physical and emotional changes. Moving from primary or prep schools often comes at this key transitional time, causing emotional upheaval at the most inconvenient period of their lives.
An all-through school provides emotional security throughout your daughter's full educational journey, especially during pivotal moments of development, helping to reduce stress and make your daughter feel secure in her environment.
8. Personalised support
Because your daughter stays in the same school environment throughout her formal education, with many of the same teachers and the ability for key stage 1 educators to communicate with later teachers, she'll benefit from more personalised experience.
From the first moment your daughter starts at an all-through school, teachers begin to understand her personality, unique learning style, strengths and areas for improvement. This information is fed through to future teachers as she progresses through school, offering a consistent and personalised learning journey.
This is not only helpful for your daughter's academic progress, but it also provides benefits for her emotional wellbeing too. Pastoral care and other support staff can monitor your daughter's wellbeing throughout her education and identify any interventions. They'll also build up strong, long-term relationships with her from Reception right up to her GCSE years.
Frequently asked questions
Are all-through schools better for girls?
All-through schools are generally better for girls because they offer a more stable and supportive educational journey. This is because girls stay in one familiar environment throughout their school years. This continuity helps girls build strong friendships, develop confidence and settle into learning routines from an early age. In all-girls all-through schools, students also benefit from learning in an environment that encourages participation, leadership and academic ambition across all subjects.
What age do girls start at an all-through school?
Girls usually start at an all-through from Nursery or Reception and remain there until Year 11 or sixth form. Starting at a younger age allows girls to become familiar with the school environment early on, helping them build confidence and feel secure as they move through each stage of their education. St Margaret's accepts pupils from Reception onwards.
Do all-through schools improve academic performance?
All-through schools are best-placed to improve academic progress by offering consistency in teaching, curriculum planning and pastoral care. Teachers can build a long-term understanding of each pupil’s strengths, learning style and development, helping pupils feel supported throughout their education. This continuity also allows students to move through key stages smoothly and focus fully on their learning.
Why do parents choose all-girls schools?
Parents often choose all-girls schools because they provide an educational environment where girls feel confident to speak up, take on leadership roles and pursue their interests freely. Girls in single-sex schools regularly achieve strong academic results and engage fully in subjects such as maths, science and sport, which they are often discouraged from in mixed-sex schools. Many parents also value the strong pastoral care and sense of community these schools provide.
Do all-through schools have entrance exams?
All-through schools like St Margaret's do not require pupils to sit additional entrance exams when moving from junior to senior school. Pupils progress naturally through the school, allowing them to focus on their learning and personal development without the pressure of preparing for another admissions process.

Our History
St Margaret’s Hampstead may not be the oldest school in the area, but it is certainly one of the oldest and has a fascinating history. Founded in 1884, it began life as one of many small, privately run schools that dotted the leafy streets of Hampstead, North London. A number of these were owned and run by unmarried women, and they often only took a handful of pupils. A great many only lasted a decade or two, closing when owners retired or passed away.
Happily, St Margaret’s not only survived, but it flourished. Today, it proudly continues its legacy in its fifth home under its fourteenth Head and has not a handful of pupils, but 160.
Our founder
Born in Perthshire, Scotland, in 1850, Elizabeth Isabella Tulloch was the second child (of 10) of a reverend. After working as a governess, as many middle-class ladies did at that time, she opened this school in a new building called Chester House in West Hampstead.
As proprietor and principal, Elizabeth led St Margaret’s for an impressive 44 years, earning praise in her final year at the school from the Board of Education Inspectors as “a women of culture and ideals to whom the school is much indebted for all her educational work”.
In 1920, Hilda Jean Copinger joined the school as joint principal, in charge of boarding and the teaching of domestic science. On Elizabeth’s retirement, in 1928, Hilda took over the school with a new co-principal, Margaret Macrae.
How St Margaret’s Hampstead got its name
The school has not always been known as St Margaret’s Hampstead, though. Like many Victorian private schools, it was simply named after its owner, so it was known as “Miss Tulloch’s” originally.
However, in 1898, a newspaper advertisement announced that Miss Tulloch would be moving the school to its second home – a house called St Margaret’s in Oak Hill Park in Barnet. While the school didn’t stay in that location permanently, the name appears to have stuck and travelled back with it to Hampstead.
In 1915, years after it had been renamed, former pupil and Rebecca author Daphne du Maurier recalled it still being affectionately known as, “Miss Tulloch’s School”. In recent years, Hampstead has been added to the end of the name to differentiate it from the numerous St Margaret’s in London and the surrounding areas.
Our school today
While St Margaret’s Hampstead is no longer a proprietorial school, we feel it has retained what we imagine was the charming, homely feel it once had when it was run by a former governess with a handful of children. It is still considered small compared to most London schools and the parents, staff and girls very much consider us one big family in a welcoming house in the heart of leafy Hampstead.
Testimonials
“Cosy, nurturing, rounded and grounded education delivered in a happy family atmosphere’’
Explore the history at St Margaret’s
We invite you to visit St Margaret's Hampstead, and experience our rich history firsthand.

Inspection Reports
We are delighted to share the outcomes of our most recent ISI inspection, which confirmed that St Margaret’s Hampstead meets all required standards. The report celebrates our exceptional pastoral care, broad and enriching curriculum, and the strong leadership and community values that underpin daily life at St Margaret’s.
Our inspectors highlighted the nurturing, inclusive environment in which every girl is encouraged to flourish academically, socially, and personally.
The Independent Schools Inspectorate (ISI) is the body approved by the Secretary of State for Education to inspect schools that are members of the Independent Schools Council (ISC). ISI inspections evaluate all aspects of a school’s provision, with a particular focus on pupils’ welfare, learning, and personal development.
Leaders and staff prioritise pupils' wellbeing, ensuring that each pupil is recognised as an individual and supported to thrive.
Pupils' emotional wellbeing and mental health are high priorities throughout the school.

pageCache.pageTitle: The House System | Curie, Du Maurier, Nightingale | St Margaret’s Hampstead
pageCache.text:
Our House System: Building Community & Leadership
At St Margaret’s Hampstead, our House System is an integral part of our pastoral care and a cornerstone of our community. It is designed to embody our core values and ethos, creating a vibrant environment where girls of all ages work together, form lasting friendships and develop a strong sense of belonging. The House System is what gives our school its unique family atmosphere, where every pupil and staff member is assigned to a House upon starting at St Margaret’s Hampstead.
Our three Houses
To create a strong sense of identity and community, every pupil and staff member is assigned to one of our three houses, each named after a notable female figure who embodies our school's values of courage, resilience and curiosity.
A place for healthy competition
Our House System nurtures a friendly competitive spirit through a variety of inter-house fixtures and competitions throughout the year. This offers every girl, regardless of her ability, the chance to represent her House and contribute to its success. We hold events including:
This emphasis on participation is a key part of our ethos. It encourages teamwork, resilience and discipline, ensuring that the benefits of belonging and healthy competition carry positive rewards into many other areas of our girls’ lives.
Sports Day
Netball competitions
House rounders.
Our Housepoint system & awards
Our girls are consistently rewarded for their hard work and dedication. Housepoints are awarded for excellent work and for exceptional performance in other areas. These points are totalled up at the end of each term for a running house total.
At the end of the academic year, the House with the highest number of Housepoints is awarded a cup, and a prize is given to the junior and senior girl who has achieved the most Housepoints overall.
Developing tomorrow’s leaders
The House System is a powerful platform for developing leadership skills. Our pupils also have a meaningful voice in school-wide decisions and gain valuable experience in leading their peers and collaborating with staff.
This helps build confidence and character, empowering our girls to take on challenges and shape the future direction of the school and beyond.
A community that connects across all ages
One of the greatest strengths of our House System is the opportunity it provides for girls of all ages to work together. It promotes what we call vertical integration, encouraging pupils from the youngest years right through to Senior School to interact, support each other and collaborate.Our unique Family Tree system, for example, is a non-competitive initiative that sits within the House System, grouping girls into small, cross-year families. In these groups, senior girls take on leadership roles, guiding younger pupils and forging genuine friendships and a network of support across all age ranges.The Houses are also a focal point for charity and fundraising events, as well as House Mufti Days and other celebrations that are run largely by the girls themselves. This further strengthens the sense of community and shared purpose.
Ready to see your daughter flourish in our caring community?
Book a tour and learn how an education at St Margaret's will transform your daughter into a confident, empowered young woman.

Music
Children who are exposed to music, or those who play an instrument, do better in school than those who don't. Researchers have found a significant relationship between music learning and positive performances in areas including reading comprehension, spelling, vocabulary, languages, mathematics, science, listening and motor skills.The act of learning and playing an instrument will enhance discipline, develop concentration and patience, help your child to socialise, increase optimism and give them a sense of pride and confidence in themselves.
Music is an important part of almost everybody’s life. As parents we strive to give our children the tools to build a successful life, and one of the best choices you can make for your children is giving them the gift of music.
Whether performing in assemblies, choirs, chamber groups or orchestras, our girls experience the thrill of music-making from an early age. Lessons take place in purpose-built teaching spaces, and our curriculum balances practical musicianship with music appreciation, composition and theory.
Specialist teaching begins in the Infant years and continues through to Senior School, where pupils explore a wide variety of genres from classical and choral to contemporary and jazz. Individual peripatetic lessons are available across a full range of instruments, supported by a strong ensemble programme that gives every girl the opportunity to perform regularly. You can book your daughters music lessons via the Parent Portal.
Through music, our girls develop the ability to listen, collaborate, persevere and perform under pressure skills that stay with them throughout life. From first notes to advanced pieces, every stage of their musical journey is supported by experienced teachers who understand how to nurture potential and inspire excellence.
Important things to consider
Carefully choose the size of your daughter’s instrument to make playing easier for her. There are nine different sizes of violins available, while guitars range from quarter size to full size. Depending on the size of your daughter’s hands, it’s best to begin with a smaller version of your chosen instrument. For example, if she is going to play guitar, choose one that will have a smaller neck, with the frets closer together (e.g., a ukulele). As your daughter grows, so can her instrument. Once you have a teacher, they can usually advise you on the right size to buy. Remember, there will be very limited progress at any age if there isn’t regular practice and enthusiasm.
Age 5 to 7 years old
As a general guideline, the piano, recorder or violin are good instruments for girls to begin learning from 5 to 7 years of age – any younger than this and a child’s fingers and hands are too small and they will struggle. In particular, starting with the piano will give your child a good foundation for future learning of any instrument. At this age, you (or someone in your household) will also have to be committed and practice with your child every time they do to help them build up good habits and enable them to progress.
Age 8 years & older
At around the age of 8, you could introduce other instruments, such as the guitar, flute, clarinet or viola. This is also a good age to start vocal lessons. At this point in your daughter’s life, you can slowly introduce independent practice to your daughter, although this depends on her personal development and levels of independence. Parents’ involvement, interest and support is always a good boost for a child's confidence. Please come to watch your daughter’s performances and encourage her to perform in front of friends and family. Also, support her in getting involved in musical groups, such as orchestra or choir, or suggest that she performs with her friends.
Ready to see your daughter discover her potential?
Music is one subject that has a positive impact on every area of your daughter’s life, from her academic performance to her confidence and creativity. Learn how the rich music curriculum at St Margaret’s Hampstead will upgrade her learning experience.

pageCache.pageTitle: Infant School Curriculum & Pastoral Care | Reception, Year 1 & 2
pageCache.text:
The Heart of Learning: Our Infant School Curriculum
At St Margaret's Hampstead, our infant curriculum for Reception, Year 1 and Year 2 is carefully crafted to provide a rich, engaging and bespoke education with one guiding principle: placing the girl at the heart of every thought and action. Our approach is a powerful synergy of exceptional pastoral care, the proven benefits of very small class sizes and an ambitious cross-curricular programme that boosts curiosity, confidence and a lifelong love of learning.
Every girl stands out at St Margaret’s hampstead
The power of personalised attention & small class sizes
With a maximum class size of 14 pupils, our Infant classrooms are uniquely positioned to offer truly individualised attention. This small scale isn’t simply a feature, it’s a philosophy. It enables our teachers to stretch, challenge and support each girl with precision and care, ensuring no child is ever overlooked.This high teacher-to-pupil ratio allows for personalised learning experiences, builds strong pupil-teacher relationships and nurtures self-esteem. It gives each girl the confidence to explore new areas of learning, take intellectual risks and develop her unique strengths to a far greater depth than might normally be possible.
Our nurturing community
We believe that a child who is happy and feels truly valued is perfectly positioned for academic and personal success. At St Margaret’s Hampstead, you’ll discover a genuine family feel – a warmth that cannot be scripted or policy-driven but is lived and felt every day.As a small school, we are able to build strong, meaningful relationships with every child. Our staff are deeply attentive and consistently listen to, support and champion each pupil. This is reflected in our most recent ISI inspection report, which praised our pupils for being "highly self-disciplined" with "excellent standards of behaviour and respect". Pupils reported highly effective pastoral care systems that help resolve issues with empathy and care.This deeply rooted sense of security gives our girls the confidence to take risks, embrace challenges and as we say often, "just have a go", knowing they will be supported every step of the way.
An ambitious & inspiring curriculum
Literacy
We use a structured, systematic synthetic phonics programme with daily sessions in Reception and Year 1, laying the foundation for fluent reading and writing. Reading is further supported through the VIPERS framework to build comprehension skills and support a love of literature.
Numeracy
Daily maths lessons from Reception focus on deep conceptual understanding, problem-solving and reasoning. We use the White Rose maths scheme and NRich resources to offer a robust, challenging and engaging learning journey.
Our bespoke infant curriculum offers comprehensive coverage of the national curriculum and the early years foundation stage, but also goes far beyond to excite, inspire and empower our pupils. Carefully planned to ensure progression across each year group, our curriculum is uniquely designed for St Margaret’s Hampstead and tailored to the needs and interests of our girls.We use half-termly themes and ‘big “I wonder…” questions’ to make learning relevant and interconnected across subjects. This thematic, cross-curricular approach helps girls make sense of the world around them, develop critical thinking skills and find joy in learning.
Outdoor learning & forest school
Learning beyond the classroom
Educational trips and real-world experiences are embedded into our curriculum to enhance classroom learning. For example, Year 1 classes visit the Science Museum’s Flight Exhibition as part of their "Explorers" topic, bringing their learning to life in exciting and memorable ways. These thoughtfully chosen visits broaden horizons, deepen understanding and help children make meaningful connections between subjects and the wider world.
The Infants’ Enrichment Programme
Our bespoke Infants’ Enrichment Programme provides a stimulating and joyful end to the school day. Designed to be both fun and challenging, the programme enriches our academic offering by allowing girls to explore their creative, physical and personal interests.
Activities include storytelling, creative arts, Lego challenges, ballet and gentle yoga. Each session is an opportunity to develop fine motor skills, social confidence and self-expression, reinforcing the belief that learning happens everywhere.
House System: our Family Trees
Every girl belongs to one of our three school houses – Nightingale, Curie and De Maurier – each named after an inspirational woman who reflects our values of courage, curiosity and compassion. Our Family Trees house system encourages collaboration and camaraderie across year groups.Girls earn house points for effort, kindness and achievement, with a house trophy awarded at our annual Prize Giving. House teams also come together for events such as Sports Day, helping to develop teamwork, resilience and school spirit.
At St Margaret’s Hampstead, our infant curriculum is more than just academic learning
It is a thoughtful, nurturing and empowering journey that ensures each girl grows in confidence, develops a love of learning and begins to understand her own unique potential.

pageCache.pageTitle: Junior School Curriculum | Years 3-6 | St Margarets Hampstead
pageCache.text:
The Junior School Curriculum: Inspiring Minds
The Junior School at St Margaret’s Hampstead is a dynamic and pivotal stage in your daughter's educational journey, designed to build on her foundational skills and prepare her for the independence of Senior School. Our curriculum is thoughtfully crafted to excite, inspire and empower every pupil through engaging half-termly themes and big “I wonder…” questions. This approach ensures that learning is active and enjoyable, helping girls make connections across different subject areas and develop a clear sense of what it means to be an expert in each discipline.
A broad & ambitious curriculum
Our syllabus ensures excellent coverage of the national curriculum for Years 3 to 6, while also providing our dedicated teachers the freedom to go above and beyond. Learning is always challenging, engaging and enjoyable, with teachers maximising opportunities for discussion, talk time and the use of our on-site facilities and outdoor spaces.
Mathematics
Children have a daily Maths lesson from Reception to Year 6, with a strong focus on developing arithmetic, reasoning and problem-solving skills. We use the latest educational resources to build a robust understanding of mathematical concepts and encourage our pupils to reason, make links and problem-solve. The emphasis is on building strong mental maths skills and a clear understanding of when to use certain operations in real-world problems.
English
In English, we use an engaging, active learning approach, giving girls extensive opportunities to develop their vocabulary, language and reading comprehension. Our approach ensures that every pupil is challenged with appropriately pitched, individualised learning to ensure they are confident readers and writers.
Science
Our Science curriculum aims to develop an enthusiasm and enjoyment of scientific learning. In weekly Science lessons, girls follow the aims of the national curriculum, building their scientific knowledge and conceptual understanding in Biology, Chemistry and Physics. Curiosity is celebrated, and girls are encouraged to ask and research their own questions, developing essential investigative and analytical skills.
Humanities
The teaching of History and Geography enriches our pupils' understanding of the world by providing an economic, political, cultural and social context. We use exciting topics, fieldwork in our local area and educational visits to make learning active and creative, helping girls to develop a well-rounded knowledge of the past and an understanding of the diverse places, people and environments around them.
Expert teaching & unique resources
In the Junior School, girls benefit from a core team of specialist teachers who are passionate about their subjects, including PE, Music, Art and Computing. These experts use our unique facilities to bring learning to life. Our girls make excellent use of our facilities, providing hands-on opportunities to develop creativity and problem-solving skills.
A nurturing environment: the power of personalised attention
Our curriculum is supported by our small class sizes, which ensure that our dedicated staff can engage with each girl on a personal level. With an average class size of around 15 students, we are able to provide a valuable level of personal attention that ensures no pupil is missed and every girl receives the support she needs to thrive. This nurturing environment is what empowers our girls to build confidence and excel to the best of their abilities.
Beyond the classroom: enriching our curriculum
Learning at St Margaret’s Hampstead extends far beyond the syllabus. We believe that immersive experiences are vital to a rich education. Our curriculum is enhanced by a range of learning opportunities, with workshops and educational visits to museums and galleries, allowing our girls to learn in different ways and deepen their understanding of the world around them.
Discover the Junior School experience at St Margaret’s Hampstead
We invite you to visit St Margaret's Hampstead and see firsthand how our Junior School empowers girls to learn, grow and thrive. Take the next step in your daughter's educational journey.

pageCache.pageTitle: Senior School Curriculum | Years 7-11 | St Margarets Hampstead
pageCache.text:
Senior School Curriculum: Empowering Futures
The Senior School at St Margaret’s Hampstead is a transformative journey from Year 7 to Year 11, designed to empower every girl to find her passions, achieve academic excellence and build the confidence to succeed in the world. Our curriculum is dynamic, challenging and engaging, with the syllabus serving as just the starting point for a deep-rooted love of learning that lasts a lifetime.
Inspiring Minds
Academic excellence & exceptional results
We are proud to offer a broad and balanced curriculum combined with ample teacher contact time, ensuring that every pupil can achieve her full potential in each academic discipline. With an average class size of around 15 students, our high teacher-to-pupil ratio means that nobody is missed and every girl receives the support she needs to excel to the best of her abilities.Our commitment to a personalised, nurturing education does not come at the expense of academic rigour. In fact, it is the direct driver of our success. We’re proud that our GCSE results have been assessed as "excellent".
Outstanding grades
In 2025, 56 per cent of all GCSE grades achieved were at grade 9-7 (A*–A equivalent).
Proven progress
Value-added data, stretching back over a decade, demonstrates that our girls "make notably more progress than pupils of similar abilities attending other schools" according to a recent Good Schools Guide report. This is the ultimate proof that our supportive environment is a direct path to tangible academic achievement.
Future pathways
Our girls are given the confidence to apply for high-achieving schools post-GCSE, with so many of them winning scholarships for their chosen Sixth Forms. We have a personalised programme of one-to-one pupil and parent consultations on the selection and application process, supporting our girls to secure their first-choice Sixth Form.
The Senior School curriculum: a broad & balanced programme
Our dynamic curriculum is designed to prepare girls for life, providing a firm academic foundation while allowing them to explore their unique interests.In addition to core subjects, all pupils choose three to four optional subjects from a wide range of disciplines, allowing them to tailor their learning to their strengths and passions.
Triple Science (three separate GCSEs in Biology, Chemistry, and Physics)
Modern Languages (French, Spanish)
A dynamic approach to learning
We believe that learning extends beyond the confines of the syllabus. Our engaging teaching methods bring subjects to life and make them relevant to the world. For example, Year 7 pupils don't just learn about Shakespeare in the classroom; they visit Shakespeare's Globe and work with actors on stage to experience a text as the writer intended. This creative and dynamic approach supports a deep-rooted love of learning for life.
Unwavering support for every girl
Our dedication to each pupil's academic journey is matched by our commitment to her wellbeing. All girls are screened for learning needs on entry to the school. Our SEND provision (special educational needs and disabilities) provides ongoing practical, emotional and academic support to girls with a range of learning needs. Our SENDCO (special education needs and disabilities coordinator) works closely with teaching staff to ensure that lessons are appropriately differentiated, and a continuous cycle of monitoring and feedback ensures every girl makes excellent academic progress.
Beyond the classroom: a world of discovery
Senior School life at St Margaret's Hampstead is rich with opportunities to explore passions and develop new skills. Our extensive co-curricular programme offers a diverse range of activities, from competitive sports and captivating performing arts to a wide array of clubs and enriching expeditions. We encourage every girl to 'have a go at everything,' developing enthusiasm and excellence in equal measure. This broad exposure helps girls build teamwork, resilience and a lifelong love for discovery, ensuring every girl stands out.
Co-curricular life: beyond the classroom
The co-curricular programme in the Senior School is the key to unlocking student potential, with a diverse range of activities that support leadership, creativity and resilience.
Academic enrichment
Clubs for ambitious academic extension include Ancient Greek, STEM, Law Society and the Biomedical Society.
Discussion & debate
Pupils can join clubs like the Model United Nations (MUN), History Discussion Group and Philosophy Club.

Bursaries at St Margaret’s Hampstead
We believe that a first-class education should be accessible to all girls from a wide range of backgrounds. We are proud to offer means-tested bursaries for financial assistance.
Our commitment to financial assistance
A bursary is a means-tested award, meaning the amount of financial assistance is determined by the financial situation of the parent or parents. For those with low income, a bursary may be awarded to cover some or all of a girl’s fees, helping to remove financial barriers to her education.
The bursary application process is thorough and designed to ensure fairness. It is also completely confidential.
To determine the level of support, an independent evaluator assesses a family’s financial situation, taking into account both income and assets. As part of this process, applicants will be required to show documentation, such as bank statements and payslips. In some cases, a home visit may also be part of the evaluation.
To be considered for a bursary, all prospective pupils must go through the same assessment process as any other applicant. This ensures that a St Margaret’s Hampstead education is a suitable fit for every girl. For entry into Year 7 and above, this includes taking the standard entrance test in English and Mathematics.
Girls applying for a bursary are not required to achieve higher than the minimum entry criteria. While bursaries are normally awarded for students in Year 7 and above, they may be offered to those in lower years if there are no suitable applicants.
The bursary application deadline is Friday 27th November 2026
How to enquire about & apply for bursaries
We encourage all prospective families to contact us directly to discuss the opportunities available for your daughter.
To begin the bursary application process, please register your daughter using the online registration form, and then contact the Bursar directly.

Leavers’ Destinations: Pathways to Bright Futures
At St Margaret’s Hampstead, our ultimate goal is to empower every girl to find her voice, discover her passions and confidently embark on the next stage of her educational journey. We take great pride in seeing our pupils transition to a diverse range of excellent schools, Sixth Form colleges, further education establishments and prestigious universities that are the perfect fit for their individual aspirations. The success of our leavers is a testament to the bespoke, high-quality education and pastoral care we provide.
Pathways after GCSEs
After completing their GCSEs at St Margaret’s Hampstead, our girls go on to attend a variety of outstanding institutions for their A Levels and other further education qualifications. Our leavers are celebrated for securing places at a wide array of institutions across the capital and beyond.
